analysis.one_liner: Requires political ads to name their top funders, including online ads and robocalls.
analysis.headline: The bill would have forced outside groups running political ads to name their top funders, but it drew no cosponsors and died in committee without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would extend the "stand by your ad" rule — the requirement that candidates appear in their own ads and approve them — to corporations, unions, and outside political groups, and require those groups to list their top funders on their ads. It would also close a loophole so that paid internet and digital ads, and prerecorded political phone calls, carry the same disclaimers as TV and radio ads. It never received a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Voters who see or hear political ads would learn who actually paid for them. Ads from groups whose funders are hidden today would have to list their top five funders on screen (or top two on audio), state who approves the message in a readable or audible way, and carry disclaimers on paid online ads and robocalls. The FEC would enforce this even before writing new regulations.

how_it_helps.text: Extends the "stand by your ad" personal approval statement to corporations, labor unions, and outside political groups, so a named person — for a corporation, the CEO — must approve the message on camera or by voice, not just a vague committee name.

Requires ads paid for by covered organizations to display a list of their top five funders (top two for audio ads), based on payments of $10,000 or more over the prior 12 months, with a website link allowed only for very short ads.

Closes the online loophole by rewriting the law so paid internet and paid digital communications count as "public communications" subject to disclaimers, with specific format rules for text, audio, and video ads on large online platforms (those with 50 million or more monthly U.S. users).
Extends disclaimer requirements to prerecorded political telephone calls and requires the disclosure statement at the beginning of such calls.

Sets readability and audibility standards — disclaimer text at least as large as the main message, audio statements at least 3 seconds, video disclaimers on screen for 4 to 6 seconds — and declares disclaimers invalid if they are hard to read or easily overlooked.

analysis.who_pays: Corporations, labor unions, 501(c) nonprofits, 527 groups, and other organizations that fund election ads would bear the cost of tracking funders, producing longer on-screen disclaimers, and having their CEO or top officer appear in ads. Large online platforms selling political ads would handle new compliance and format rules. Donors whose names would appear as top funders lose anonymity.
analysis.who_pays_short: Dark money groups and major ad platforms

drawbacks.text: The definitions are broad and could reach beyond obvious election spending: a "covered transfer" can include ordinary payments a covered organization makes to another group that later does political spending, which could impose disclosure duties or chilling effects on charities, trade associations, and civic groups engaged in ordinary granting or business activity.

The top-funder lists reflect all payments of any type a group received over 12 months, not just the money behind the specific ad, so a listed "top funder" may have had nothing to do with that advertisement — disclosure that could mislead as much as inform.

Only online platforms with 50 million or more monthly U.S. users are covered by the special digital rules, leaving ads on smaller websites, apps, and newsletters subject to different or lighter treatment.
The rules would take effect January 1, 2022 without waiting for Federal Election Commission regulations, which could create uncertainty about exactly how groups and platforms must comply at first.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The voter benefit — knowing who pays for the political messages aimed at them — is real and cheap to deliver; the main costs are compliance burdens on advocacy organizations and platforms, plus some definitional overreach that could sweep in groups with only indirect ties to electioneering. The bill contains carve-outs (ordinary business transactions, segregated accounts, small political committees) but its breadth and reliance on FEC rulemaking would have made early enforcement messy.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House committee that handles election matters, never got a hearing or a vote, and expired when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative David Price, a North Carolina Democrat, introduced the Stand By Every Ad Act on February 18, 2021.
The bill was referred the same day to the House Committee on House Administration, the committee with jurisdiction over election and campaign finance rules.
No other member signed on as a cosponsor.
The committee never took the bill up — the action record shows no hearing, markup, or floor action after the referral — and the bill died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Organizations that spend on federal elections without naming their funders kept the status quo, and no member of Congress ever had to take a recorded position on disclosure. Voters got nothing; the information the bill would have required stays hidden.

for.name: Rep. David Price
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and became its only sponsor; no other member signed on.

against.name: House Committee on House Administration
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction over campaign finance and election rules
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on the day it was introduced and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on it during the two-year Congress.

against.name: Rep. Zoe Lofgren
against.role: Chair, House Committee on House Administration
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, never brought the bill to a markup or vote; the committee took no action on it.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and the bill had a single Democratic sponsor with zero cosponsors from either party, so no partisan split can be measured.

industries.industry: Dark money political groups (501(c) nonprofits, 527 organizations, and outside spending vehicles)
industries.note: These groups exist in large part to run election ads without naming their donors. The bill would force their ads to carry a top-funders list and a named approver, ending the anonymity that makes them useful conduits for undisclosed money.

industries.industry: Corporations and labor unions spending on elections
industries.note: Both would become "covered organizations" whose election ads must name the top officer who approves the message and list top funders. Unions' dues-based transfers get some accommodation, but both lose the ability to advertise through lightly labeled vehicles.

industries.industry: Online platforms and digital ad sellers
industries.note: Large platforms (50 million or more monthly U.S. users) selling political ads would face new disclaimer format, labeling, and hyperlink requirements, a compliance cost — but the rules also formalize online political advertising as a mainstream, regulated channel, which the industry can operate under.

industries.industry: Political advertising and media (broadcasters, cable, ad agencies)
industries.note: Existing TV and radio disclaimer rules would be extended and made stricter (longer on-screen time, audibility standards), modestly raising production costs, while robocall advertising would face new disclosure duties at the start of each call.
